challenges.name: edge-cases-quiz
challenges.title: Which learner does this code fail?
challenges.description: Two pieces of the streak code an AI assistant wrote for the CodeDev profile page: how it turns a timestamp into a day, and what it returns for a learner with no completions.

questions.explanation: False. toISOString() always formats the instant in UTC, so both completions become "2026-10-20": the same day, counted once. For Linh they are on 20 and 21 October, two days of a streak. Whatever the server's or the test machine's time zone is, this code computes UTC calendar days, which match local days only for learners at UTC+00:00 - and the demo data and the developer's own test were exactly that. The fix is to shift the instant by the learner's offset before taking the date (or to use the learner's time zone explicitly). The misconception is that an ISO string with a date in it is "the date" of the event; a calendar day only exists relative to a time zone.

True. Math.max() with no arguments returns -Infinity (the identity value for a maximum), and the type number allows it, so tsc does not complain. JSON has no Infinity, so JSON.stringify writes -Infinity (and Infinity and NaN) as null. The profile API then sends longest: null to the page, which may show "null days" or crash on a call such as .toFixed(). The empty input is the first edge case to test, and the cheapest: start from an explicit value instead, for example runs.reduce((a, b) => Math.max(a, b), 0). Spreading has a second edge: with a very large array, Math.max(...runs) can throw a RangeError because every element becomes a function argument. The misconception is that a function that works for every non-empty example also works for none.

challenges.name: learning-streaks
challenges.title: Learning streaks that survive time zones
challenges.description: The CodeDev profile page shows a learner's current and longest learning streak: consecutive local calendar days with at least one completed lesson. The version an AI assistant wrote passed its demo and broke for learners in UTC+07:00, for learners who study twice a day and for learners who study late at night. Write computeStreaks(completedAt, offsetMinutes, now). completedAt: lesson-completion timestamps in ISO 8601 with an offset ("2026-10-21T06:30:00+07:00", "2026-10-20T23:30:00Z"), in any order, possibly several per day, never later than now; ignore any entry for which Date.parse returns NaN. offsetMinutes: the learner's fixed UTC offset in minutes (420 = UTC+07:00, -300 = UTC-05:00, 330 = UTC+05:30; between -720 and 840; no daylight saving time). now: the current instant (ISO 8601, always valid). The local day of an instant is its calendar date at UTC + offsetMinutes; a day counts when at least one completion falls on it. Return { current, longest }: longest = the greatest number of consecutive counted days (0 when none), current = the length of the run of consecutive counted days that ends on the local day of now or the day before (the streak survives until the end of today), otherwise 0. Up to 5000 timestamps. Do not use Intl or the runner's own time zone (getDate, getHours, toDateString): the offset is the only time zone. The test runner reads { cases: [{ completedAt, offsetMinutes, now }] } as JSON and prints one { current, longest } per case. You may use an AI assistant; the hidden tests check the edges.
hints: Before writing any loop: what is the "day" of a completion for a learner at UTC+07:00, and is it the same as the date you can read in the ISO string? Then list the inputs that would break a first version: none, two on one day, out of order, one minute either side of local midnight, and "not yet today".

Turn every valid timestamp into one integer, the learner's local day number: take the instant from Date.parse, add the offset in milliseconds, and divide by the length of a day, rounding down. Whole day numbers make "consecutive" a comparison with previous + 1 - no months, no leap years. Put them in a Set, then sort the distinct day numbers before you walk them once.

A similar trace with offset -300 (UTC-05:00): "2026-03-01T03:00:00Z" is 22:00 on 28 February local, "2026-03-01T14:00:00Z" is 09:00 on 1 March, "2026-03-03T01:00:00Z" is 20:00 on 2 March. Local days 28 Feb, 1 Mar, 2 Mar: one run of 3. With now = "2026-03-04T02:00:00Z" (21:00 on 3 March) the run ends yesterday, so it is still current; with now = "2026-03-05T05:00:00Z" (00:00 on 5 March) the last counted day is three days back and the current streak is 0, while the longest stays 3.
